newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: NZ SPORT - Others jealous of All Blacks - Hart.
newsitem.headline: NZ SPORT - Others jealous of All Blacks - Hart.

text.p: PRETORIA, July 17 - Political games and outbursts against the All Blacks from Australia and South Africa show that jealousy is creeping into the Southern Hemisphere rugby scene, says All Black coach John Hart.
Hart was holding little back as he countered accusations by the Wallabies and the Springboks that his team employed illegal tactics to kill their opponents' game.
"I think this All Blacks side is a special side," Hart said.
"I think when you get something special everyone wants to knock it whatever way they can. Some jealousy is creeping in.
"I think there's some jealousy about our scrum and it's something we can be quite proud of quietly."
Hart believes teams are resorting to sledging, politics and means beyond the spirit of the game to try and stop the All Blacks from winning.
"Yes, I think there's a bit of that," he said to suggestions that the All Blacks' opponents were turning to off-field tactics in an attempt to stop their success.
Hart said he felt sad over the way Australia were attacking Englishman Ed Morrison for his refereeing during the first Bledisloe Cup match in Christchurch two weeks ago.
The All Blacks beat the Australians 30-13 and Wallabies coach Greg Smith later accused the home side of using professional fouls.
Hart reacted then by reprimanding one of his players, Robin Brooke, as he had committed one such offence.
However he also said he had watched a video of the match and picked out three occasions when the Australians had used the illegal tactics to stop the All Blacks from scoring tries.

Hart appeared to lose his patience at the continuous outbursts against his team, after hearing Australian Rugby Union chief executive John O'Neill had repeated that he would have "severe words" with Morrison before the second Bledisloe Cup test in Melbourne on Saturday week.
"We can't have him replaced but we need to have some severe words with him," O'Neill has been quoted as saying.
Hart said he was saddened and disappointed by O'Neill's attack on the referee.
"We as coaches and players should be trying to help the referee, not the reverse," Hart said.
"It can have an impact on referees, which is a bit sad."
It appeared, Hart suggested, that the Australians and the South Africans were making an orchestrated effort to influence or intimidate referees.
South African coach Carel du Plessis said he would talk to Sunday's (NZ time) tri-series test ref, Australian Peter Marshall, about the All Blacks' professional fouls.
"I'm confident that Marshall and his supporting touch judges will hold everything under control," Hart said.

The New Zealand coach will meet Marshall to clear up the professional foul issue and will counter the South Africans' claims by informing the referee that he believed the Springboks would resort to physical intimidation during the test.
